nature.headline: Study finds primate conservation shields thousands of other species
nature.tease: Protecting primate habitats could serve as an efficient shortcut for saving broader biodiversity.
nature.summary: Protecting primates may be one of the most efficient ways to protect biodiversity overall, a new study finds. Researchers analyzed the habitats of 16 primate species in China's Yunnan province alongside 601 threatened and endemic animal species and 4,010 plant species. They found that designating just 30% of Yunnan as a primate conservation priority would protect about a third of the habitat for 86% of the animals and 72% of the plants studied — plus more than half the province's annual carbon storage. Because primates need large, healthy stretches of forest, saving space for them shelters countless other species too.
nature.deeper:
Primates make good 'umbrella species' — protect enough forest for them, and you end up sheltering the whole neighborhood. Researchers mapped this out in China's Yunnan province, home to 16 primate species, and found that setting aside less than a third of the land for primates would cover a meaningful share of habitat for hundreds of other animals and thousands of plants, plus a large chunk of the region's carbon storage.

It's not just about geography. Primates disperse seeds by eating fruit and dropping it elsewhere, so they help keep forests regenerating. Conservationists say their decline is often an early warning sign — when primates vanish from a forest, it's usually already in trouble. They're also easier to raise money for than, say, a beetle or a fungus, since people care about charismatic animals.

This isn't a new idea — groups protecting gorillas in Congo and orangutans in Borneo and Sumatra have made similar arguments, estimating tens of thousands of species could benefit. Experts note the approach works well in practice; the real obstacles are political and human, not conceptual. Still, it's a reminder that saving one much-loved species can be a shortcut to saving many others.

discovery.headline: AI helps scientists identify bird species in radar migration data
discovery.tease: New AI tools turn fuzzy radar blobs into detailed maps of migrating bird species.
discovery.summary: Scientists have built a tool that can tell which bird species are migrating through a stretch of sky, something weather radar alone could never do. BirdFlow combines millions of birdwatcher observations from the eBird app with weather radar data and AI to map where specific species are likely headed week by week. Radar has long shown flocks as unidentified blobs. Researchers from Cornell, the University of Massachusetts, and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign tested BirdFlow against 30 years of radar data and built models for 153 North American species. That species-level detail could help protect threatened birds, reduce building and aircraft collisions, and track disease spread among wild and farmed birds.
discovery.deeper:
For decades, radar showed migrating birds as dark, shapeless clouds. Useful for spotting a wave of movement, but useless for knowing which birds were actually flying. BirdFlow fixes that by pairing radar with something humans are already good at: birdwatching. Millions of sightings logged through the eBird app helped researchers figure out which species were likely present in those radar blobs, and when.

Cornell researcher Yuting Deng described asking a simple weekly question: given where a species was last week, how likely is it to be in a nearby location this week? Repeated across a season, that builds a route.

Why it matters: conservation groups can now focus efforts on the specific species passing through at a given time. Aviation managers can watch for larger birds that risk colliding with planes. Cities running lights-out campaigns to stop birds crashing into buildings can target the groups most at risk. And because BirdFlow can track where birds go after visiting an area, agencies are already interested in using it to watch how avian diseases might spread from wild birds to poultry farms.

progress.headline: Australia sets $31.30 minimum wage for gig delivery drivers
progress.tease: A new industrial ruling gives delivery drivers guaranteed pay and injury insurance nationwide.
progress.summary: Delivery drivers across Australia will now earn a guaranteed minimum of $31.30 an hour, under new standards approved by the Fair Work Commission. The rules also require delivery platforms to provide personal accident insurance for workers, while keeping the flexibility gig work is known for. The change came after the Transport Workers' Union joined forces with DoorDash and UberEats to jointly request the protections, following years of talks. Officials and union leaders called the result "world-leading," and it's expected to apply broadly across on-demand food, drink, and grocery delivery platforms, offering a safety net to hundreds of thousands of workers.
progress.deeper:
For years, gig delivery work has meant unpredictable pay — riders and drivers might wait unpaid for a restaurant order, with no guarantee of a minimum wage or protection if they got hurt on the job. That's changing in Australia. Starting in August, delivery platforms must pay workers a guaranteed hourly rate, and organise insurance that covers them if they're injured while working.

What makes this notable is how it came together: the union representing gig workers didn't fight the platforms alone in court — it worked with DoorDash and UberEats to jointly propose the new rules to the industrial umpire. Both sides gave a little. Workers are now called "employee-like" rather than full employees, and they'll need to insure their own vehicles against damage to others. In exchange, they get steady minimum pay and injury cover, without losing the flexibility to choose their own hours.

It's a rare case of a gig economy fight ending in a shared framework rather than a standoff. Officials are calling it a milestone, and it's likely to be watched closely elsewhere, since similar gig-work disputes are playing out in many countries.

animals.headline: Detection dogs help scientists study rare, elusive species
animals.tease: Trained dogs sniff out scat, opening a window into secretive wildlife like black-footed cats and pangolins.
animals.summary: In South Africa's Karoo, two German Shorthaired Pointers named Lyka and Sebala are sniffing out scat from some of the region's hardest-to-study animals, including black-footed cats and Temminck's pangolins. Working with conservation biologist Michelle Schroeder, the dogs have found hundreds of samples in months, work that took a human researcher over a year to match on her own. Each scat carries genetic clues about an animal's sex, health, diet, and relationships to others nearby. That data is helping scientists estimate population sizes, track gene flow across the landscape, and even flag habitats worth protecting from development.
animals.deeper:
Some animals are just hard to see. Black-footed cats hide in burrows by day and leave droppings almost anywhere, with no pattern to follow. Pangolins are nocturnal, camouflaged, and their droppings vanish within a day or two. So researchers turned to dogs, whose noses can pick up what humans simply can't.

Michelle Schroeder's dogs, Lyka and Sebala, found in a few months what she'd spent over a year searching for alone. Each dropping they find holds what she calls "nuggets of genetic data" — enough to tell researchers an animal's sex, sometimes its identity, and how populations connect across the landscape. Early results from the Karoo suggest black-footed cats there still have healthy genetic diversity and can move freely between areas, though researchers caution this may not hold everywhere.

The same approach is helping protect riverine rabbits, too. When dogs and camera traps confirmed rabbits were living in land proposed for wind-energy projects, it gave conservationists solid evidence to push back on development in sensitive habitat.

The work isn't glamorous, and funding is tight — a pangolin tracking project stalled this year for lack of money. But for Schroeder and her colleagues, the dogs are more than tools. They're partners who, when the fieldwork ends, get to just be dogs again.
